newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro-bourses fall but largely ignore Deng.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro-bourses fall but largely ignore Deng.

text.p: Several European bourses went into retreat on Thursday, led by a sharp correction in Germany, but markets outside Asia largely ignored the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
The dollar was bid up in early European trading with Deng's death having a muted impact, but the currency eased against the mark following publication of a strong business climate report in Germany.

European markets focused mainly on local factors, while Asian investors reacted to Deng's long-expected death by marking prices higher in China, Hong Kong and Taiwan following wild swings at the start of Asian business.

"It wouldn't be true to say it passed without incident as far as the market was concerned because the dollar did react," said one Zurich-based foreign exchange dealer. "But overall the price action has been slight."
Traders in Europe were concerned about economic data coming out of Germany, however.
The German Bundesbank reported its main monetary policy indicator, M3 money supply, grew strongly in January, which economists said dampened further any hopes of another interest rate cut.
Then the country's Ifo economic institute said its west German business climate index jumped to 93.3 in January from 90.9 in December, indicating that business confidence was increasing.
And German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt predicted Europe's largest economy would continue to recover this year.

"We are standing by our forecast of 2.5 percent economic growth," Rexrodt told parliament during a debate of the government's annual economic report. "The German economy has been back on the growth track since the spring of 1996. All indications show that will continue in 1997."
Despite the bullish sounds from Rexrodt, German shares started trading sharply down, although they later lifted off their lows.
"We haven't had really negative numbers but I suppose people are thinking now that it can't get better than this. And we really need to clear the air here," said a Frankfurt dealer.

Wall Street's weak performance overnight weighed on the market, while jitters ahead of Friday's expiry of options contracts added to the volatility. Dealers said the feeling on the market was that prices had been pushed up to unrealistic levels.
By 1015 GMT, the 30-share DAX index had fallen 1.3 percent to 3,191 points, although government bonds were trading off their lows and the dollar was lending support.
With no change in German interest rates expected at the Bundesbank's policy-making council meeting during the morning, the dollar reacted to the strong Ifo report by easing a little.

The dollar was bid up to around 1.7000 marks in early trade before declining to around 1.6875, compared with Wednesday's European close of 1.6979. Against the yen, it touched 124.62 after the news of Deng before falling back to around 123.73.
London shares opened the day below their record close on Wednesday, but later recouped their losses to show small gains by mid-morning.
"... If Wall Street opens weaker this afternoon, we'll come off a bit," said one dealer following the 47 point fall in the Dow Industrials overnight.
Yet analysts said the underlying tone of the market remained positive, with British inflation subdued, economic growth relatively strong and the gilt market generally firm.
"We could still see a squeeze in a liquidity-driven market. But it's a bit of a junkie bull market. We need a diet of good news to go higher," the dealer added.
French stocks opened lower as the market continued to digest its recent gains.
"It's a small consolidation and it's occurring calmly," a trader said. "None of the blue chip CAC issues is losing much more than two percent. It's profit taking affecting the whole of the market."
Although the CAC-40 index was down 16 points at 2,578 by 1015 GMT, traders said the bourse's weakness did not put in doubt the market's broadly rising trend.
Credit Lyonnais certificates shot up seven percent to around 200 francs after Les Echos newspaper said that the state-owned bank expected to report a big increase in profits in 1997.
Shares in Thomson-CSF lost 0.8 percent of Wednesday's 3.7 percent gains following the government's announcement that it would privatise its 58 percent stake in the firm through a trade sale.
CURRENCIES AT 1015 GMT
The dollar was quoted as 1.6875 marks and 123.73 yen, compared with 1.6979 marks and 124.35 yen in late European trading on Wednesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1015 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 3.4 points, or 0.08 percent, at 4,360.8.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 16.02 points, or 0.62 percent, at 2,578.74.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 42.05 points, or 1.3 percent, at 3,191.70.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold opened lower at $345.20, down from $346.55 on Wednesday. Silver was steady at $5.19.
